items.question: What interested you about approaching translation between languages with very different syntactic structures as an optimization problem?
items.object: Syntax-based machine translation as an optimization problem
items.answer: I've always been interested in language. That was what drew me to the field to begin with. My dissertation work is on syntax and translation, and in particular I'm interested in how you would translate between two different languages that have very different syntactic structure. During my PhD, I was interested in this topic from the point of view of optimization. I was very interested in how we could rephrase problems of, say, translating from English to Japanese in terms of a mathematical program. A lot of the work I did at that point was thinking about things like integer linear programming, how you come up with new algorithms, how you make this all efficient in practice. In retrospect, that does seem like a kind of far cry from where NLP has ended up, but at the time this was an important problem in the field. I actually did an internship at Google to implement some of this stuff in their production systems, and it was really important that we take a sentence, come up with syntactic structure, and use that for all sorts of downstream tasks. That's where the field was at the time. I was fascinated by that sort of area, but it certainly moved in a very different direction.

items.question: How do you now view your earlier belief that complex inference would remain central to NLP?
items.object: The roles of learning, inference, and data in NLP
items.answer: The history of NLP had been, even at that point, a kind of bounce back and forth between the importance of learning and the importance of inference. The particular area of machine translation was always one where data was critically important, and there's very famous work that looked at learning basically from scratch how to do translation. I've certainly always been on the learning side of things. I think maybe where I went wrong is I thought that inference was really a critical part of the process, and that complex inference that utilized learned models to make predictions was critically important. One way you can think about this is, when AlphaGo came out, a lot of that was advanced learning, but it still had a lot of inference, like Monte Carlo tree search. I was interested in the Monte Carlo tree search part of NLP at the time, and I thought that would play a larger role going forward. I think maybe what I didn't predict was just how much data there was in NLP and how just learning more and more on that data would make things better.

items.question: How do you think NLP research should balance engineering larger models with exploring new architectures and core deep learning questions?
items.object: The balance between engineering and architectural innovation in NLP research
items.answer: I don't think of myself as particularly conservative. I think I understand the importance of engineering and building large models. It's something I'm passionate about, but I think he's really on the extreme in the sense of thinking that almost everything we should be doing is really on the engineering side of the equation. I still think that it's very possible there will be a significant shift in core questions about deep learning, and that we should have an environment where people feel comfortable working on things that aren't just making models larger or making them more efficient. Probably most emblematic of this is the fact that he and I have a long bet. A couple years ago we made a bet about whether Transformers would continue to be the dominant architecture in NLP after five years. We're about two years into that bet, and I think he'll likely win it. I think they'll likely stick around for the next three years, but I think it represents my optimism about the possibility of architectures.

items.question: How do you think decisions about the direction of NLP research should be made?
items.object: Bottom-up control of research
items.answer: I'm a strong believer in bottom-up control as opposed to top-down control of research. I do think what's critically important is building environments and spaces where people feel comfortable trying new things, to encourage new ideas. I think part of the reason I feel this way is from my early work in NLP and feeling like I didn't predict well enough where things would go. I felt like a lot of the work that was being done in deep learning didn't feel like it had a home either in a machine learning or an NLP context, and I think we should have been more willing to accept it, work with it, and understand its constraints at that time. That's a general philosophy.

items.question: What kind of research community are you trying to create through the Conference on Language Modeling, or COLM?
items.object: Conference on Language Modeling (COLM)
items.answer: In terms of how we get there, I'm putting my time where my mouth is. Recently I've been working with a bunch of researchers to establish a new conference, which we're calling the Conference on Language Modeling, or COLM. The goal of that conference is to think about the main topics that we think are very interesting for the future of language modeling, and to establish an academic community where people are free to work on them and build new systems. We put out a call for papers, and if you go through the topics you can see that they're pretty different than what's traditionally studied in natural language processing and also pretty different than what's studied in ICLR. So we think this is a new space for working on these topics and where they move going forward. One thing that's been particularly interesting about this process is that the program chairs are a combination of academics and people in industry.

items.question: How do you think a research environment should support people pursuing different research directions?
items.object: Research environments that support different directions of research
items.answer: Speaking from the context that I'm aware my experience may not be the same as everyone else's, I think the key first idea is getting a group of people together, listening to different ideas, bringing people in from different backgrounds or different perspectives to try to help in that process itself. From there, my goal has been to acknowledge that in research you're trying to build a portfolio of different ideas. We don't know that one idea is going to work out 100% of the time, and so it's okay for people to take these 5% bets and see where they head. That all being said, I do think it's important that researchers get feedback, get real about their results, have empirical measures and goals that they're working to as a community. I think it is important that people agree on what those are, at least so there's some sort of ground truth that the community can be working towards.

items.question: What makes state space models an alternative to Transformers that you find worth pursuing?
items.object: State space models as alternatives to Transformers
items.answer: I've been interested in exactly this question of what architectures besides Transformers might work out. I've been particularly fascinated by a class of architectures called state space models. They have a mathematical maturity and understanding of how they work, as well as promising initial results and very nice efficiency properties. That combination of ideas has made them a topic of interest for me. I've been following the work of Albert Gu, who's now a professor at CMU, on this topic. I recently put together a tutorial that went over how they work and how they are used. The short story is that they're basically a type of model that's mathematically equivalent to a linear recurrent neural network, like an RNN that you may have been used to from the 2015 period, but you remove the nonlinearity, so there's no tanh or ReLU as part of the recurrence. Because you do that, you're able to run them much more efficiently in practice, and they run basically in a similar way as running a convolutional neural network. Because of that, they run very efficiently on modern hardware, particularly during training but also during inference. That's a very nice property that gets rid of a lot of the issues that running Transformers at large scales encounter. Because of all this I've been really interested in building this. We recently built a version that replicates the performance of BERT on many tasks, and we've been working on another version for diffusion models. Other folks have been working on trying to scale these up to the size of large language models. I don't know if this is going to work out; it might be that Transformers are too ingrained in the culture right now, but I'd really like to see these other architectures thrive.

items.object: Tri Dao's combination of technical skill and intellectual curiosity
items.answer: One other point on this front is that another researcher I've encountered in the process is Tri Dao, who's going to be a professor at Princeton next year. I think he embodies something I really think is important for a modern graduate student: he's really good at the low-level technical details, but also a curious thinker and willing to try out all sorts of different ideas. If you can get both of those skills together, you can really build some cool things.

items.question: What do you find promising about state space models as alternatives to Transformers?
items.object: State space models as alternatives to Transformers
items.answer: In the perfect world, you get a model that's a state space model that has exactly the same number of parameters as, say, Llama 7 billion. Let's say it works actually at the same performance level. That's a big if, but I think it's possible. Now that you have this model, you're in a really good position. One thing that's really nice about it is it entirely doesn't require any storage of keys and values. If you've ever tried to implement Llama, you'll know that one of the most annoying parts is the key-value cache and actually keeping that around and making it efficient in practice. In this kind of theoretical model, that entirely goes away. You also have near-infinite history. This is assuming that you're able to learn enough from the history to make it useful, but you can start to imagine having extremely large context lengths and keeping track of a tremendous amount of few-shot examples. With the caveat that this would have to work as well, it starts being a really nice and convenient model, both from its theoretical sense and from the fact that it would be really useful in practice.

items.question: How do you think state space models might affect the lost-in-the-middle problem observed in Transformers with very long contexts?
items.object: State space models and the lost-in-the-middle problem in long-context Transformers
items.answer: Yeah, I think it's an open question, and we'll have to see what happens when people scale these approaches. The big question is whether that property is emerging because of the way that we train these models, in which case this doesn't really help, or if it's some fundamental property of the architecture. My guess is it's a property of the data and the tasks we train on, and not anything to do with the actual architecture itself. That being said, it'll be interesting to see what these trade-offs actually look like in practice. In general, I would really like to have another reference model so that we can make deeper statements about how these problems arise.

items.question: Do you think studying probabilistic context-free grammars still has substantial value for someone doing NLP research today?
items.object: The value of studying probabilistic context-free grammars in NLP research
items.answer: Frankly, probably not. I still think context-free grammars are a really elegant formalism, and if you're thinking about them in the context of cognitive science or linguistics, or trying to understand language in a deeper sense, then absolutely. But if you're trying to actually use them in practice, I consider it basically a solved problem. For me personally, it was always a means to an end. I believed that we needed to first solve PCFGs before we could move forward on NLP, and so that's the reason I initially studied it. That being said, I will defend the grammar-induction paper: it's about how you induce context-free grammars from raw language. I think that's an interesting and fascinating problem that connects to cognitive development and how languages work, even if it's not central for making better NLP systems.

items.question: How do you view the significance of your work on sequence-level knowledge distillation?
items.object: Sequence-level knowledge distillation
items.answer: I think I'm going to look back at this as probably one of the most important projects I've worked on. At the time, I didn't think about that at all. We were playing around particularly with machine translation models, and we just wanted to try knowledge distillation, which seemed to work really well for images. On machine translation, the problem we ran into was that it didn't work very well for language. We tried to distill the distribution of next-word prediction, just like it was in an ImageNet model. We tried to take a big model and learn a small model's next-word prediction by copying it. Since that didn't work that well, we thought of other ways to do it, and the main idea we came up with was that we should be matching the distribution at the sequence level. That is, try to replicate the teacher's full translation, not just its individual words. Because of that, we came up with an approach where we generated from the teacher, regenerated all the training data, and then trained a small model on that data, and it worked extremely well. In fact, in this paper we ran some experiments on my Android phone. We were able to run translation on the phone, which was really exciting at the time. The paper kind of went away until recent years, when people have been very fascinated by this idea of knowledge distillation. We're seeing this apply to all sorts of different models. Just last week we released a model that distilled Whisper, the OpenAI speech recognition system, basically using a very similar approach, and it worked really well. We were able to speed up Whisper by about five times and actually run it in the web browser. We're also seeing ways that people are using GPT-4 for distillation, methods like Alpaca that produce sequences you can train smaller models on using this approach. It turned out to be a simple, basic idea, but it works in a lot of different applications.

items.question: Why do you think sequence-level knowledge distillation works better than approximating a large model’s word-level distributions?
items.object: Sequence-level knowledge distillation
items.answer: My hypothesis in the paper was that when you generate a sequence there's interdependencies between decisions, and what you really want to approximate is the large model's distribution over sequences. Think about this like an extremely large space where instead of predicting words you're predicting whole translations or responses. That's a very complex distribution, and it's hard to approximate with simple word distributions. To get around this problem, in this paper we argue that one approximation is to simply take the argmax or to take multiple samples from the big model. That's obviously a very raw approximation of the full space, but if you can do that in a clever way, either by using a filter to direct the process or trying to use additional knowledge, you can do a relatively good approximation and then copy that with your smaller model.

items.question: What kinds of model-efficiency research do you find intellectually interesting?
items.object: Research on model efficiency
items.answer: From a research perspective, I sometimes get a little bored with efficiency work because we know that there's a bunch of these tricks that work really well, kind of combinations of them. I'm not a big fan of papers of that form. I think we should think about new and creative ways to make models more efficient. One thing I'm interested in these days is how you can make fine-tuning more efficient, in the sense of backprop is just extraordinarily expensive for memory reasons. What are wild ideas for how you train without doing backprop? For instance, there's a recent paper on zero-order training of models that only use the forward paths for training. I don't know if I would use that, but it's a cool and pretty different idea. Similarly, ideas like LoRA or prompt tuning, all these things that took a different tack to try to solve some of the efficiency problems people were dealing with in practice.

items.question: How do you approach trying to understand what is happening inside language models when they perform in-context learning?
items.object: Interpreting the internal workings of language models and in-context learning
items.answer: I very much appreciate that people are trying, but I've moved out of the game of trying to interpret the internals of these models. They're beyond me. The dimensionality is so high, and I've seen so many surprising results that I no longer try. I know that's not a satisfying answer, but I'm so interested in GPT-4. It's so good, but I can't see its insides. I don't even know how many parameters it has. I've stopped trying to guess what's happening.

items.question: How do you assess the prospects and value of mechanistic interpretability research?
items.object: Mechanistic interpretability research
items.answer: I've had amazing conversations with people in that community, and I remain agnostic about whether they'll achieve their goals. I appreciate so much the energy they've brought to it and the community they've built. It feels a little bit to me like tilting at windmills, but I'm for a broad and open bottom-up effort on these approaches. I've appreciated reading a lot of the papers in that space. I'll particularly call out some of the recent work they did to try to understand grokking. I found that to be a very interesting and non-trivial way of looking at that problem. I enjoyed reading about it. I don't know whether I came out of that paper feeling more or less optimistic. It felt like even at that small a scale it was nearly impossible to prove things to a degree I felt comfortable with, but I really appreciate the effort.

items.question: What do you see as the main contribution of your paper “Multitask Prompted Training Enables Zero-Shot Task Generalization”?
items.object: “Multitask Prompted Training Enables Zero-Shot Task Generalization” and T0
items.answer: This was a paper that was part of the BLOOM project, a large open-source, multi-group collaboration. Almost 500 people were involved. It was one of the subgroups in that project and one of the more interesting research projects I've worked on. We had a team of folks get together and basically just write prompts for every task in NLP. We sat down and wrote them, and doing that was an extremely large effort. We had to decide how to do version control, how to build debugging tools, how to make everything work nicely together, and collect a group of people who were pretty divergent in their interests and goals. I think that model was quite interesting. The model that came out of that was called T0, and it showed ways of doing what we call instruction tuning these days on lots of different tasks. In practice, I think the main contribution there was showing that this kind of instruction tuning works, and doing it in an extremely rigorous way. What is it useful for now? I think it's still widely used as a source of these prompts, and it was helpful to understand the accuracy on different tasks.

items.answer: One thing that changed in the last couple years is that people moved on from standard NLP tasks to much weirder, more conversational, more realistic task benchmarks. I think that's been positive for the field, although it's made it harder to do evaluation and understand how good models are.

items.question: What makes “How Many Data Points Is a Prompt Worth?” an example of the kind of research you love doing?
items.object: “How Many Data Points Is a Prompt Worth?”
items.answer: It was basically one researcher with one question. We weren't trying to understand how prompting worked; we were trying to answer a single empirical question: If you do training on top of a prompt, how many fewer supervised points do you need? In this context, we were training a T5-style model where we gave it a prompt to start with, and we found that we could precisely quantify exactly the number of training points you got by specifying the task in words. This is a simple idea. I think we knew that prompting worked, but this is the kind of research I really love to do, where we were able to come to an answer by running a large set of carefully controlled empirical experiments. We didn't answer anything about the internals of the model, just the question of, if you are trying to annotate data, is it worth it to write down the task you're doing? We found that on a small scale, yes; on a large scale, maybe no, but we could give an exact answer to that question.

items.question: How has your view of controlling language models through prompting changed over the last year?
items.object: Controlling language models through prompting and self-criticism
items.answer: Yeah, man, it's really changed over the last year. This was obviously an area I was extremely interested in in the T5 era. These days, it seems like you can get an extraordinary amount of control by simply coming up with good prompts. Things like reflection-based models or self-criticism seem to work really well: you just feed your model its input back in and keep iterating till you get something like what you want. To that point, I'm pretty happy with many of the control applications I'm interested in.

items.question: What kind of precise control over language-model outputs do you still want researchers to pursue?
items.object: Classifier-constrained language generation and diffusion models
items.answer: I still love this idea that you could have a classifier and generate some outputs that are as high quality as a GPT model but satisfy precisely the classifier's output value. It seems like people have been able to do this with diffusion models, and I love a lot of the work going on with diffusion models for language that try to satisfy control properties like this. It's still not 100% working, but it's an area I hope people continue exploring. I'll call out Jang Lisa Lee, who's at Stanford, doing cool work in this space.

items.question: Why are you interested in attributing language-model predictions to their training data?
items.object: Attributing language-model predictions to training data
items.answer: The other thing I'm particularly interested in these days is attributability: the ability to train a large language model and know what part of its training data led to a given prediction. I think that's related to control, or at least what we thought about in terms of control in the past: knowing that a certain phrase or output came from some training data. We are very far from being able to do that with really good models.

items.question: How do you view retrieval augmentation as a way to trace a language model’s output to specific data?
items.object: Retrieval augmentation and attribution in language models
items.answer: If I had a company and I had to do this stuff right now, I would certainly look at some sort of retrieval augmentation. That seems to be the best way to ensure that certain aspects of your output come from some specific type of data. But I do come down on the side that I think that's probably a hack. I don't mean that in a negative way, but I feel like the ideal model is one that both ingests the data and is also able to know and refer to specific aspects in its history. I've heard people argue that that might be impossible for certain reasons, but I don't know why people are so negative about that. It doesn't feel like— I don't know, it feels like you should be able to have a single monolithic model that's able to also recall that it is reciting some fact from some document.

items.question: How do you see the relationship between research on controlling language models and concerns about existential AI safety?
items.object: Language-model control research as a response to existential AI safety concerns
items.answer: I tend to find the conversation about existential safety very challenging to connect to research. I'm impressed that folks have been able to do it, but to me they feel like pretty different parts of my brain. I am interested in control as a problem. I certainly do not think that the way to solve societal fears about AI and language models is by PCA on the vector space of the seventh layer. That being said, I think that work is really good, and the results seem solid, although it needs more research, more scale, and to be tried on more problems itself. I just find it a disconnect when I see claims that a small change to a vector in a giant model could somehow control the safety risk of an entire system.

items.question: Why do you recommend the experience of having your established research interests challenged, as yours were at Facebook AI Research?
items.object: Being pushed away from syntactic parsing during a postdoc at FAIR
items.answer: I mentioned that I worked on syntax for my dissertation. I was very interested in syntactic parsing and translation. I graduated in 2014 and got myself a postdoc at FAIR, so this is a Facebook AI Research group. I got into FAIR and I was like, “I'm gonna work on parsing,” and they're like, “No, you're not. That's silly.” I said, “No, no, that's what I work on. That's what I do,” and they were like, “Nope, we don't do that. We don't care about that.” I really recommend everyone, once you get to the point you're confident, to have that experience. Feeling like you're totally lost, totally in the wrong place, just out to lunch, really makes you rethink things and start over.

items.question: How did learning Torch and then using PyTorch change your understanding of research and teaching?
items.object: Torch and PyTorch as tools for research and teaching
items.answer: The way I started over was I started to learn Torch. Torch at that time was written in Lua, and it was a real hassle, but it was really eye-opening. Even at that point it was extraordinarily good. I built a model that year that was an abstractive summarization model that we published in 2015. It was one of the first neural summarization approaches. To build that, I had to learn this structure and learn how it worked. After graduating, I started as a professor and wanted all my students to have that experience, so I had them learn Torch, and a lot of my teaching was just teaching them how this worked. By about 2017, PyTorch came out, and frankly it was just a revelation. It was the first time I felt I could connect research and coding in such a direct way: I could express things I'd only thought of mathematically almost directly into code, and code that ran extraordinarily fast. I really credit the work that the open-source team did for changing my whole research agenda and understanding how this new and different way of thinking about the world worked. I've always been extremely inspired by them and what they've done with PyTorch. I think it's one of the most important projects I've ever seen, and because of that I try very hard to understand and teach how it works. I've developed my teaching here at Cornell Tech almost entirely around PyTorch. I teach a course where we use a project I built called MiniTorch, where each student basically builds their own little PyTorch through each homework assignment. We cover autodifferentiation, tensors, GPU programming, and build real models using their version of Torch at the end. Anyway, I think maybe other people have different experiences. I've always been interested in that.

items.question: How do you think about the purpose of your PyTorch-related open-source projects?
items.object: Rush's open-source projects exploring PyTorch
items.answer: In practice, I think all my open-source projects are ways for me to explore the boundaries of where PyTorch goes. Named Tensor was about thinking about different ways to add safety to the language. TorchStruct, a different project, looked at how you would build classical NLP models like hidden Markov models or context-free grammars in PyTorch. Recently I've been building a lot of puzzles that are ways for people to learn about different mathematical topics by playing with little PyTorch toys. The most recent one looked at distributed training, where people actually build pipelines or different sorts of complex distributed training architectures in a little PyTorch-like language.

items.question: How do you think deep learning libraries should serve users with very different needs?
items.object: Deep learning libraries for different audiences
items.answer: In practice, I assumed that every person doing machine learning would have to code in this language, but more and more I realize that there are very different audiences. The person whose job it is to do DeepSpeed is very different from an undergraduate learning about how MNIST classification works. Because of that, heterogeneous tools for how to build these systems might be necessary. I know that Torch has done a remarkable job being one tool for everyone, although I certainly think cracks have shown over the years when people try to scale it. I feel like Google has done a better job of building a tool that works at very large scales but is a little intimidating for entry-level users.

items.question: Where do you think the right abstraction level lies for programming with large language models?
items.object: Programming interfaces and abstraction levels for LLMs
items.answer: I'm maybe becoming more and more convinced that the next big question in open source is not how people use and build neural networks but how people utilize LLMs. The last year has been exciting to see so many different programming interfaces for how people build RAG systems, build prompt systems, and connect databases and large language models. In some sense, I almost feel like maybe the abstraction barrier was previously drawn too low, and that at least from an NLP perspective it might be possible that the abstraction will be a little bit higher. I think the abstraction needs to be lower than the OpenAI API, so open models give us a way to rethink what coding with LLMs is. I don't think I've seen yet the perfect interface where I feel super in control to express all the LLM programs I want to build.

items.question: How do you understand your shift from building NLP systems toward a more empiricist research style?
items.object: The shift from building NLP systems toward an empiricist research style
items.answer: I think I thought of myself for many years as a systems builder. I was particularly interested in how to craft new architectures and algorithms to solve tasks. That was really what most motivated me, and it's still the thing that I get most excited about. The introduction of the Transformer and then BERT really forced me to go through a lot of these growing-pains questions pretty early on. Even by 2021 it became clear to me that the sort of work I used to do was no longer really the most pressing thing. I thought a lot about other approaches. I have written several papers in the past about the internals of models, trying to understand and change the way models work, but I think the change in style came about just from frustration with how challenging it was. I didn't really want to publish results I didn't feel like I believed. I got motivated by a lot of nice papers I was reading that came at it from a more scientific angle—not in a positive sense, but in the sense of: this problem is really hard, we need to collect a lot of data, draw some curves, and be honest about the error bars. Papers like “How Many Data Points Is a Prompt Worth?” or a recent paper we're presenting at NeurIPS in a couple weeks, on scaling data-constrained language models, come about from trying a lot of experiments, drawing graphs, trying to figure out how these properties work, and trying to make predictions from this empiricist point of view. I think it comes not from a true belief but honestly from uncertainty and feeling like this stuff is hard and maybe we won't understand it exactly.
